title: Case report: chronic relapsing cryptococcal meningitis in a patient with low mannose-binding lectin and a low naïve CD4 cell count
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man was referred to our neurology clinic after 3.5 months of relapsing, diffuse headaches lasting several days, one episode of nausea and vomiting, a 15-minute period of diplopia, and intermittent back and shoulder pain. He denied fever but reported sporadic night sweats. His medical history was unremarkable, and neurologic examination findings were normal. 

Initial MRI showed cerebellar edema and extensive leptomeningeal enhancement. A lumbar puncture revealed an opening pressure of 25 cm H2O, pleiocytosis (325 leukocytes/μl), and elevated protein (990 mg/L). Tests for tuberculosis (IGRA, tuberculin skin test, and CSF PCR) were negative.

He was referred with a differential of malignancy versus central nervous system infection. CT scans of the chest and abdomen, as well as a total-body PET scan, showed no evidence of malignancy. Repeat MRI demonstrated new leptomeningeal lesions with reduced cerebellar edema and focal contrast enhancement at L5–S1. A second lumbar puncture (June 2015) showed 301 cells/μl (predominantly polyclonal T-lymphocytes) and low CSF glucose (2.3 mmol/L). Serologic testing excluded HIV, Treponema pallidum, and Borrelia infection. Because his symptoms were mild and no diagnosis was reached, no empirical treatment was initiated.

At 3- and 9-month follow-up visits, he was clinically well and MRI findings had normalized. In August 2016, he returned with persistent mild headaches, disorientation, dizziness, and palpitations. Physical and neurologic examinations remained unremarkable, but MRI revealed new nodular leptomeningeal enhancement. A PET scan remained negative for focal FDG uptake, and a follow-up MRI in February 2017 showed a slight increase in meningeal contrast enhancement. In March 2017, an extended effort was made to detect malignant cells in the CSF and to further exclude infectious causes.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Metastatic carcinomatous meningitis was considered because of leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI but was excluded because “No signs of malignancy were observed on CT abdomen and thorax as well as on total body PET scan.”  
2. Tuberculous meningitis was considered in light of chronic meningitis and CSF pleiocytosis but was excluded because “Examinations for tuberculosis (IGRA, tuberculin skin test, PCR on CSF) were negative.”  
3. Neurosyphilis and neuroborreliosis were considered but were excluded because “Serology was performed which excluded HIV, Treponema pallidum and Borrelia infection.”  
4. Lymphomatous meningitis was suspected due to relapsing nodular leptomeningeal lesions on MRI — “MRI findings pointed towards a relapsing lymphoma as the cause of his symptoms” — but was excluded because “no malignant cells were observed.”
